topic: everyday science facts (why the sky is blue, how vaccines work, what causes tides)
prompt: Why is the sky blue?
treated: The sky is blue because sunlight is scattered by the molecules that make up the air, and this scattering is far stronger for shorter wavelengths of light than for longer ones. Sunlight looks white but is actually a mixture of all the colors of the spectrum, from red at the long-wavelength end to blue and violet at the short-wavelength end. As this light travels through the atmosphere, it collides with nitrogen and oxygen molecules, which redirect it in all directions. Because the amount of scattering rises sharply as the wavelength gets shorter, blue light is scattered many times more than red light. This scattered blue light comes at you from every part of the sky rather than straight from the sun, so when you look up, the whole dome of the sky glows blue.
plain: The sky is blue because air molecules scatter sunlight, and shorter blue wavelengths are scattered much more strongly than longer red wavelengths. That scattered blue light reaches your eyes from all over the sky, so it looks blue.

topic: everyday science facts (why the sky is blue, how vaccines work, what causes tides)
prompt: How do vaccines work?
treated: Vaccines work by training your immune system to recognize a specific germ before you ever encounter the real, dangerous version of it. A vaccine introduces a harmless piece or weakened form of a pathogen into your body, something that carries the germ's identifying features but cannot make you sick. Your immune system treats this as a genuine threat and mounts a response, producing antibodies tailored to that pathogen and generating memory cells that record what it looks like. Because those memory cells persist long after the vaccine is gone, your body remembers the germ. If you are later exposed to the actual pathogen, the immune system recognizes it immediately and responds fast enough to stop the infection before it can make you seriously ill.
plain: Vaccines work by exposing your immune system to a harmless piece or weakened form of a germ, prompting it to make antibodies and memory cells. If the real germ later shows up, your body recognizes it and fights it off quickly before it makes you seriously ill.

topic: everyday science facts (why the sky is blue, how vaccines work, what causes tides)
prompt: What causes tides?
treated: Tides are caused by the gravitational pull of the Moon, and to a lesser extent the Sun, acting on Earth's oceans. The Moon's gravity tugs hardest on the side of Earth facing it, pulling the ocean water there into a bulge. At the same time, a second bulge forms on the opposite side of Earth, because that side is pulled toward the Moon less strongly than the solid Earth is and effectively gets left behind. As the Earth rotates on its axis each day, any given coastline passes through these bulges, which is why most places experience two high tides and two low tides daily. The Sun adds its own smaller gravitational effect, and when the Sun and Moon line up their pulls combine to make especially large tides.
plain: Tides are caused mainly by the Moon's gravity pulling on Earth's oceans, raising a bulge of water on the side facing the Moon and another on the opposite side. As Earth rotates, coastlines pass through these bulges, giving two high and two low tides a day. The Sun's weaker pull adds to this, and larger tides occur when the Sun and Moon align.

topic: everyday science facts (why the sky is blue, how vaccines work, what causes tides)
prompt: Why do we have seasons?
treated: We have seasons because Earth's axis is tilted relative to the plane in which it orbits the Sun. This tilt stays pointed in the same direction in space throughout the year, so as Earth travels around the Sun, each hemisphere leans toward the Sun for part of the year and away from it for the other part. When a hemisphere is tilted toward the Sun, sunlight strikes it more directly and the days are longer, delivering more energy and producing summer. When that same hemisphere is tilted away, sunlight arrives at a shallower angle and the days are shorter, so it receives less energy and experiences winter. Because the two hemispheres always lean in opposite directions, they have opposite seasons at the same time.
plain: Seasons happen because Earth's axis is tilted as it orbits the Sun. When a hemisphere tilts toward the Sun, it gets more direct sunlight and longer days, making summer; when it tilts away, it gets shallower sunlight and shorter days, making winter. The two hemispheres tilt opposite ways, so their seasons are opposite.

topic: everyday science facts (why the sky is blue, how vaccines work, what causes tides)
prompt: Why does ice float on water?
treated: Ice floats on water because it is less dense than the liquid water beneath it. In most substances the solid form is denser than the liquid, but water is unusual: when it freezes, its molecules lock into an open, ordered crystal structure held together by hydrogen bonds, and this arrangement spaces the molecules farther apart than they are in liquid water. Because the same number of molecules now takes up more room, a given mass of ice occupies a larger volume than the same mass of liquid water. Density is mass divided by volume, so the greater volume makes ice less dense. An object that is less dense than the fluid around it floats, which is why ice cubes rise to the top and ice forms on the surface of lakes.
plain: Ice floats because it is less dense than liquid water. When water freezes, its molecules form an open crystal structure that spaces them farther apart, so the ice takes up more volume than the same mass of liquid. Being less dense than the water around it, the ice floats.

topic: everyday science facts (why the sky is blue, how vaccines work, what causes tides)
prompt: Why does the Moon appear to change shape over the month?
treated: The Moon appears to change shape over the course of a month because we see different amounts of its sunlit half as it orbits Earth. The Moon does not produce its own light; it shines only by reflecting sunlight, so at any moment exactly one half of it is lit while the other half is dark. As the Moon travels around Earth, the angle between the Sun, the Moon, and our viewpoint keeps changing, so we see the lit half from different directions. Sometimes we face the fully lit side and see a full moon, sometimes we face the dark side and see almost nothing, and at in-between positions we see only a portion of the lit half as a crescent or half shape. This cycle of changing views is what we call the phases of the Moon.
plain: The Moon changes shape to us because it shines by reflecting sunlight, so half of it is always lit. As it orbits Earth, we view that lit half from different angles, seeing anything from a full moon to a thin crescent. These changing views are the Moon's phases.

topic: everyday science facts (why the sky is blue, how vaccines work, what causes tides)
prompt: What causes the ocean's tides?
treated: One of the most common questions people ask about the ocean is what actually causes the tides to rise and fall each day. The explanation lies in the pull of gravity from the Moon and, to a lesser extent, the Sun. The Moon's gravity tugs on the Earth's water, pulling the oceans into a bulge on the side of the Earth facing the Moon. At the same time, a second bulge forms on the opposite side of the Earth, which produces high tides in two places at once. As the Earth rotates on its axis, different locations pass through these bulges, which is why coastal areas experience high and low tides at regular intervals throughout the day. Said differently, the water level rises where the bulges are and falls in the areas between them, and the spinning of the planet moves each shoreline through this pattern. The Sun's gravity adds to this effect, strengthening the tides when the Sun and Moon line up. So tides are caused by the gravitational pull of the Moon and Sun on the Earth's oceans, combined with the Earth's rotation.
plain: Tides are caused by the gravitational pull of the Moon and, to a lesser extent, the Sun on the Earth's oceans. The Moon's gravity creates a bulge of water on the side facing it and another on the opposite side, and as the Earth rotates, each coast passes through these bulges, producing high and low tides.

topic: basic programming questions with one standard answer (what a hash map is, what git rebase does)
prompt: What is a hash map?
treated: A hash map is a data structure that stores data as key-value pairs, allowing you to associate each unique key with a corresponding value. The core idea behind it is that it uses a hash function to convert each key into an index, and that index determines the location in an underlying array where the associated value is stored. Because the position is computed directly from the key rather than found by searching, this design is what gives a hash map its defining performance characteristic: it provides average-case constant-time O(1) complexity for insertion, deletion, and lookup operations. When you want to retrieve a value, the same hash function is applied to the key to recompute the index, so the map can go straight to the right slot. Together, these mechanics make the hash map a structure built around fast, direct access to values through their keys.
plain: A hash map is a data structure that stores key-value pairs. It uses a hash function to convert a key into an index into an underlying array, where the value is stored. This provides average-case constant-time O(1) complexity for insertion, deletion, and lookup. To retrieve a value, the same hash function is applied to the key to recompute the index.

topic: basic programming questions with one standard answer (what a hash map is, what git rebase does)
prompt: What does git rebase do?
treated: Git rebase is a command that moves or reapplies a sequence of commits onto a new base commit, and understanding what that means requires looking at how it operates. Rather than simply combining branches, it takes the commits from your current branch and replays them one by one on top of the target branch's latest commit. In the process of replaying them, it creates new commits with new commit hashes, because each commit is being rebuilt on a different foundation than before. The overall effect of this replaying is that it produces a linear project history, avoiding the extra merge commit that a merge would otherwise create. For that reason, rebase is commonly used to keep a feature branch up to date with the main branch by reapplying the feature branch's work on top of the latest main.
plain: Git rebase moves or reapplies a sequence of commits onto a new base commit. It replays the commits from your current branch on top of the target branch's latest commit, creating new commits with new commit hashes. This produces a linear history and avoids a merge commit. It is commonly used to keep a feature branch up to date with the main branch.

topic: basic programming questions with one standard answer (what a hash map is, what git rebase does)
prompt: What is the difference between a stack and a queue?
treated: A stack and a queue are both linear data structures that hold a sequence of elements, but they differ in the order in which elements are removed, and that ordering rule is what fundamentally distinguishes them. A stack follows the Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) principle, which means the most recently added element is the first one to be removed; its two primary operations reflect this, with push adding an element to the top and pop removing the element from the top. A queue, by contrast, follows the First-In-First-Out (FIFO) principle, so the earliest added element is the first one removed; its operations are enqueue, which adds an element to the back, and dequeue, which removes an element from the front. In short, the stack works from a single end while the queue adds at one end and removes from the other, and this difference in access order is the essential distinction between them.
plain: A stack follows Last-In-First-Out (LIFO), where the most recently added element is removed first, using push to add to the top and pop to remove from the top. A queue follows First-In-First-Out (FIFO), where the earliest added element is removed first, using enqueue to add to the back and dequeue to remove from the front. The difference is the order in which elements are removed.

topic: basic programming questions with one standard answer (what a hash map is, what git rebase does)
prompt: What is recursion in programming?
treated: Recursion in programming is a technique in which a function solves a problem by calling itself, and the way it works is by breaking a larger problem down into smaller instances of the same problem. Each of these smaller instances is handled by another call to the same function, and this continues until the problem is small enough to be answered directly. That point is handled by the base case, a condition that stops the recursion and returns a result without making any further calls, which is essential because it prevents the function from calling itself endlessly. The part that keeps the process moving is the recursive case, where the function calls itself on a smaller version of the problem. Together, the base case and the recursive case make recursion work, since one guarantees the process eventually ends while the other progressively reduces the problem toward that ending point.
plain: Recursion is a technique where a function solves a problem by calling itself on smaller instances of the same problem. It requires a base case, a condition that stops the recursion and returns a result without further calls, and a recursive case, where the function calls itself on a smaller version of the problem. The base case prevents the function from calling itself endlessly.

topic: basic programming questions with one standard answer (what a hash map is, what git rebase does)
prompt: What is the difference between '==' and '===' in JavaScript?
treated: In JavaScript, both == and === are used to compare two values, but they differ in how strictly they perform that comparison, and this distinction matters for how results are determined. The == operator is the loose equality operator, and its defining behavior is that it performs type coercion: if the two values have different types, it converts one of them so that both share a common type before comparing them. The === operator is the strict equality operator, and it takes the opposite approach by performing no type coercion at all; it returns true only if the two values have both the same type and the same value. Because of this difference, an expression like 5 == '5' evaluates to true, since the string is coerced to a number, while 5 === '5' evaluates to false, because the two operands are of different types and no conversion is applied.
plain: In JavaScript, == is the loose equality operator, which performs type coercion by converting values to a common type before comparing them. === is the strict equality operator, which performs no type coercion and returns true only if the values have the same type and value. For example, 5 == '5' is true, but 5 === '5' is false.

prompt: What is a primary key in a relational database?
treated: A primary key in a relational database is a column, or a combination of columns, that uniquely identifies each row in a table, and this role of unique identification is what defines its purpose. To fulfill that role reliably, a primary key must satisfy two requirements: its values must be unique across the table, so no two rows can share the same primary key value, and its values cannot be null, because a null could not serve to identify a row. As a consequence of enforcing these requirements, each table can have only one primary key. That single primary key is also what enables tables to be linked together, since it can be referenced by a foreign key in another table, establishing a relationship between the two tables.
plain: A primary key is a column or combination of columns that uniquely identifies each row in a table. Its values must be unique and cannot be null. A table can have only one primary key. It can be referenced by a foreign key in another table to establish a relationship between the two tables.

topic: settled history and geography facts
prompt: What is the capital of Australia?
treated: The capital of Australia is Canberra. Although many people assume the capital is Sydney or Melbourne because those are the country's largest and most internationally recognized cities, the capital is in fact Canberra. Canberra was purpose-built to serve as the seat of government, and it was chosen precisely as a compromise between the rival cities of Sydney and Melbourne, each of which had wanted the honor for itself. Because neither city could be allowed to prevail over the other, a new city was planned and constructed on land set aside for that role, and it is there that Australia's federal government resides.
plain: The capital of Australia is Canberra. It was purpose-built as a compromise between Sydney and Melbourne, which both wanted to be the capital, and it serves as the seat of the federal government.

topic: settled history and geography facts
prompt: What is the longest river in the world?
treated: The longest river in the world is the Nile. Flowing through northeastern Africa, the Nile extends for approximately 6,650 kilometers, a length that carries its waters across multiple countries before they reach the Mediterranean Sea. Along that long course the river passes through or borders several nations, drawing on tributaries and drainage from a wide region of the continent. It is this immense length of roughly 6,650 kilometers, combined with its northward journey to the Mediterranean, that establishes the Nile as the longest river on Earth.
plain: The longest river in the world is the Nile. It flows through northeastern Africa for about 6,650 kilometers before reaching the Mediterranean Sea.

topic: settled history and geography facts
prompt: Who was the first person to walk on the Moon?
treated: The first person to walk on the Moon was Neil Armstrong. He set foot on the lunar surface on July 20, 1969, during NASA's Apollo 11 mission, the flight that first carried human beings to a successful landing on the Moon. As he stepped down onto the surface, Armstrong spoke the famous words, "That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind," a phrase that marked the moment humanity first stood on another world. It was in that role, as the Apollo 11 astronaut who descended first, that Neil Armstrong became the first human to walk on the Moon.
plain: The first person to walk on the Moon was Neil Armstrong. He stepped onto the lunar surface on July 20, 1969, during the Apollo 11 mission, saying, "That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind."

topic: settled history and geography facts
prompt: Which country has the largest population in the world?
treated: As of 2023, the country with the largest population in the world is India. For many decades China had held this position as the most populous nation, but in 2023 India surpassed China to take the top spot. Both countries have populations exceeding 1.4 billion people, placing them far ahead of every other nation, yet it is India that now holds the larger of the two. This shift in 2023 made India the world's most populous country, ending China's long-standing status at the top.
plain: As of 2023, the country with the largest population in the world is India. It surpassed China that year, with both nations exceeding 1.4 billion people.

topic: settled history and geography facts
prompt: What event marked the beginning of World War II in Europe?
treated: The event that marked the beginning of World War II in Europe was Germany's invasion of Poland on September 1, 1939. When German forces crossed into Poland on that date, they set in motion the chain of events that started the war on the continent. In direct response to this invasion, Britain and France declared war on Germany two days later, on September 3, 1939, honoring their commitments to Poland. It was this sequence—the invasion of Poland followed by the British and French declarations of war—that opened World War II in Europe.
plain: World War II in Europe began with Germany's invasion of Poland on September 1, 1939. In response, Britain and France declared war on Germany on September 3, 1939.

topic: settled history and geography facts
prompt: On which continent is the Sahara Desert located?
treated: The Sahara Desert is located on the continent of Africa. Stretching across the northern portion of Africa, it is the largest hot desert in the world, covering an enormous expanse of the continent's landmass. Its vast area spreads across numerous countries in North Africa, reaching from one side of the continent toward the other. Because of this sweeping presence across northern Africa, the Sahara stands as the world's largest hot desert and firmly places itself on the African continent.
plain: The Sahara Desert is located in Africa. Spanning northern Africa across many countries, it is the largest hot desert in the world.

topic: settled history and geography facts
prompt: Which country was the first to send a human into space?
treated: When considering which nation first achieved the milestone of sending a human into space, the answer is well established. The first country to send a human into space was the Soviet Union. This happened in 1961, when cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin completed an orbit of the Earth aboard the Vostok 1 spacecraft. To put it another way, it was the Soviet Union that put the first person beyond the boundary of space, with Gagarin as the individual who made that flight. So the nation credited with this historic first is the Soviet Union, thanks to Gagarin's 1961 orbital journey aboard Vostok 1.
plain: The Soviet Union was the first country to send a human into space, when cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin orbited the Earth aboard Vostok 1 in 1961.

topic: how common household or mechanical things work
prompt: How does a toilet flush?
treated: A toilet flushes by suddenly emptying the water stored in its tank into the bowl, and this rush of water is what carries the waste away. When you press the handle, a chain lifts a rubber flapper that sits over the opening at the bottom of the tank. With the flapper raised, the tank water pours rapidly through that opening into the bowl below. This fast surge of water fills the bowl and pushes the contents over the curve of the trap, and once the water starts flowing over that bend it pulls the rest along in a siphon that empties the bowl. As the tank drains, the flapper falls back down and seals the opening again. A float inside the tank drops with the falling water level, which opens the fill valve so fresh water refills the tank until the float rises back to its set level and shuts the valve off, leaving the toilet ready for the next flush.
plain: Pressing the handle lifts a flapper in the tank, releasing the tank water into the bowl. This surge pushes the contents over the trap and starts a siphon that empties the bowl. The flapper then reseals, a float drops and opens the fill valve, and the tank refills until the float rises and shuts the valve off.

topic: how common household or mechanical things work
prompt: How does a refrigerator keep food cold?
treated: A refrigerator keeps food cold by moving heat out of its interior and releasing it into the room, using a refrigerant that circulates in a loop. The process begins at the compressor, which squeezes the refrigerant gas and raises its pressure and temperature. This hot gas then travels through the condenser coils on the outside of the fridge, where it gives off its heat to the room air and cools into a liquid. The liquid refrigerant next passes through an expansion valve, where the sudden drop in pressure makes it turn cold. This cold refrigerant flows through the evaporator coils inside the fridge, where it absorbs heat from the food and air in the compartment, which is what keeps the inside cold. Absorbing that heat turns the refrigerant back into a gas, and it returns to the compressor to repeat the cycle. In this way heat is continually pumped from inside the fridge to the outside.
plain: A refrigerator moves heat from inside to the room using circulating refrigerant. The compressor pressurizes the refrigerant into a hot gas, which sheds heat in the condenser coils and becomes liquid. An expansion valve drops its pressure, making it cold, and it absorbs heat from inside via the evaporator coils. This turns it back to gas, and it returns to the compressor to repeat.

topic: how common household or mechanical things work
prompt: How does a zipper work?
treated: A zipper works by using a slider to interlock two rows of teeth into a single joined strip, and to pull them apart again. Each side of the zipper has a row of teeth, and every tooth has a hook on top and a hollow underneath. The slider is the small piece you pull, and it is shaped inside with a wedge that splits into two channels. When you pull the slider upward, its channels guide the teeth together so that the hook of each tooth settles into the hollow of the tooth from the opposite side, locking them in an alternating pattern that holds firmly. When you pull the slider downward, the wedge inside forces between the joined teeth and pries them apart, separating the two rows. So the same slider both fastens and unfastens the zipper depending on which way you move it.
plain: A zipper has two rows of teeth, each tooth with a hook and a hollow. The slider you pull is shaped with a wedge and channels. Pulling it one way guides the teeth together so each hook seats into the hollow of the opposite tooth, locking them alternately; pulling it the other way forces the wedge between the teeth and pries them apart.

topic: how common household or mechanical things work
prompt: How does a thermos keep drinks hot or cold?
treated: A thermos keeps drinks hot or cold by slowing down every way that heat can travel between the drink and the outside, and its main trick is a vacuum. It is built as a container with double walls, and the space between those two walls has had the air pumped out to create a vacuum. Because heat conduction and convection both need matter to carry the heat, and a vacuum has almost no matter, very little heat can pass across that empty gap. This means a hot drink stays hot and a cold drink stays cold for much longer. The walls facing the vacuum are also given a shiny, mirror-like coating, which reflects radiant heat back instead of letting it pass through, blocking the one path that does not need matter. Together the vacuum and the reflective surfaces cut off conduction, convection, and radiation, so the drink's temperature changes very slowly.
plain: A thermos has double walls with a vacuum between them. Since conduction and convection need matter to move heat, the near-empty vacuum blocks them, so a hot drink stays hot and a cold one stays cold. The walls also have a mirror-like coating that reflects radiant heat back, blocking the remaining path. Together this slows conduction, convection, and radiation.

topic: how common household or mechanical things work
prompt: How does a manual can opener work?
treated: A manual can opener works by combining a sharp cutting wheel with a gripping gear to slice around the rim of a can while pulling itself along. You clamp the opener onto the edge of the can so that a small sharp wheel presses down and punctures the metal lid just inside the rim. Facing that cutting wheel is a toothed wheel that grips the underside of the can's rim like a gear. When you turn the handle, the toothed wheel bites into the rim and rotates, and because it holds the rim it drags the whole opener around the circle of the can. As the opener travels, the sharp wheel keeps slicing through the lid along the way. By the time you have turned the handle all the way around, the cut has gone completely around the top and the lid comes free.
plain: You clamp the opener so a sharp wheel punctures the lid just inside the rim, with a toothed wheel gripping under the rim opposite it. Turning the handle rotates the toothed wheel, which grips the rim and drags the opener around the can while the sharp wheel slices the lid. One full turn cuts all the way around and frees the lid.

topic: how common household or mechanical things work
prompt: How does a toaster brown bread?
treated: Many people wonder exactly how a toaster manages to brown a slice of bread, and the answer comes down to a fairly simple electrical process. Inside a toaster are wires made of a special alloy called nichrome, which is a combination of nickel and chromium. When you push down the lever and switch the toaster on, electricity flows through these nichrome wires. Because nichrome has a high electrical resistance, it resists the flow of that electricity, and this resistance causes the wires to heat up and glow. To put it another way, the electrical energy is converted into heat energy as the current struggles to pass through the resistant metal. That heat radiates onto the surface of the bread, and it toasts the outer layers of the slice, driving off moisture and browning the surface through a reaction between sugars and amino acids in the bread. In short, a toaster browns bread by running electricity through high-resistance nichrome wires that heat up and radiate that heat onto the bread.
plain: A toaster browns bread by running electricity through nichrome wires, an alloy of nickel and chromium. Because nichrome has high electrical resistance, it heats up and glows as current passes through it. That radiated heat drives off moisture and browns the bread's surface through a reaction between its sugars and amino acids.

topic: how common household or mechanical things work
prompt: How does a flush toilet empty the bowl?
treated: A common question about everyday plumbing is how exactly a flush toilet manages to empty the bowl of water and waste. The mechanism relies on something called a siphon. When you press the handle, water is released quickly from the tank into the bowl, raising the water level rapidly. Beneath the bowl there is a curved pipe shaped like an upside-down U, known as the siphon tube. As the water level rises quickly, water fills this curved tube completely. Once the tube is full, it begins to pull water and waste over the bend and down the drain. In other words, the filled siphon creates suction that drags the contents of the bowl through the pipe. This suction continues until the bowl is nearly empty and air enters the tube, which breaks the siphon with a characteristic gurgle. To sum up, a flush toilet empties the bowl by rapidly releasing tank water that fills a curved siphon tube, and the resulting suction pulls the bowl's contents down the drain.
plain: A flush toilet empties the bowl using a siphon. Pressing the handle releases tank water quickly into the bowl, raising the level fast. This fills the curved, upside-down-U siphon tube beneath the bowl, and once full it creates suction that pulls water and waste over the bend and down the drain. The siphon breaks with a gurgle when air enters the tube.

topic: arithmetic, units and simple quantitative reasoning with one right answer
prompt: How many centimeters are in 2.5 meters?
treated: To convert from meters to centimeters, we rely on the fact that one meter is defined as exactly 100 centimeters. This means that every meter we have contributes 100 centimeters to the total, so converting simply requires scaling by that factor. Starting with 2.5 meters, we multiply the number of meters by 100 centimeters per meter. Carrying out that multiplication, 2.5 times 100 gives us 250. Therefore, 2.5 meters is equal to 250 centimeters.
plain: One meter equals 100 centimeters, so 2.5 meters is 2.5 times 100, which is 250 centimeters.

topic: arithmetic, units and simple quantitative reasoning with one right answer
prompt: If a car travels 150 miles in 3 hours, what is its average speed?
treated: Average speed is defined as the total distance traveled divided by the total time taken to travel that distance. In this case, the car covers a distance of 150 miles over a period of 3 hours, so these are the two quantities we need to combine. Setting up the calculation, we divide the 150 miles by the 3 hours to find how many miles are covered in each single hour. Performing that division, 150 divided by 3 equals 50. Therefore, the car's average speed is 50 miles per hour.
plain: Average speed is distance divided by time, so 150 miles divided by 3 hours equals 50 miles per hour.

topic: arithmetic, units and simple quantitative reasoning with one right answer
prompt: What is 15% of 80?
treated: To find a percentage of a number, we first recognize that a percentage is a fraction out of 100, so 15% means 15 per 100, which can be written as the decimal 0.15. Once we have that decimal form, finding 15% of a quantity is simply a matter of multiplying the quantity by it. Here the quantity is 80, so we multiply 80 by 0.15. Carrying out that multiplication gives 12. Therefore, 15% of 80 is 12.
plain: 15% equals 0.15, and 80 times 0.15 is 12, so 15% of 80 is 12.

topic: arithmetic, units and simple quantitative reasoning with one right answer
prompt: How many seconds are in one hour?
treated: To determine the number of seconds in an hour, we build up from the standard units of time. One hour is made up of 60 minutes, and each of those minutes in turn contains 60 seconds. Because every minute contributes 60 seconds, the total number of seconds in the hour is found by multiplying the 60 minutes by the 60 seconds in each minute. Performing that multiplication, 60 times 60 equals 3,600. Therefore, there are 3,600 seconds in one hour.
plain: One hour is 60 minutes and each minute is 60 seconds, so 60 times 60 gives 3,600 seconds in an hour.

topic: arithmetic, units and simple quantitative reasoning with one right answer
prompt: A recipe needs 4 eggs to serve 6 people. How many eggs are needed to serve 9 people?
treated: This is a proportion problem, so we keep the ratio of eggs to people constant while scaling up the number of people served. The original recipe uses 4 eggs for 6 people, which tells us how many eggs each person's share requires. Dividing 4 eggs by 6 people gives two-thirds of an egg per person. To serve 9 people, we multiply that per-person amount by 9, computing two-thirds times 9, which equals 6. Therefore, 6 eggs are needed to serve 9 people.
plain: The ratio is 4 eggs for 6 people, or two-thirds of an egg per person, so 9 people need two-thirds times 9, which is 6 eggs.

topic: arithmetic, units and simple quantitative reasoning with one right answer
prompt: How many kilograms are in 3,500 grams?
treated: Converting from grams to kilograms depends on the fact that one kilogram is defined as exactly 1,000 grams. Because each group of 1,000 grams makes up a single kilogram, we can find how many kilograms we have by dividing the total number of grams by 1,000. Starting with 3,500 grams, we divide that figure by 1,000 grams per kilogram. Carrying out the division, 3,500 divided by 1,000 equals 3.5. Therefore, 3,500 grams is equal to 3.5 kilograms.
plain: One kilogram equals 1,000 grams, so 3,500 grams divided by 1,000 is 3.5 kilograms.

topic: definitions of well-established terms in economics, biology and law
prompt: In economics, what is opportunity cost?
treated: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative that a person gives up when making a choice. Because resources such as time, money, and labor are limited, choosing to use them in one way necessarily means they cannot be used in another way. Every decision therefore involves a trade-off, and the opportunity cost captures what is sacrificed by not pursuing the most valuable option that was forgone. It is not the sum of all the alternatives that were passed over, but specifically the single best one among them. By focusing attention on this forgone alternative, opportunity cost provides a way of measuring the true cost of a decision in terms of what could have been gained instead, which is why it is central to how economists think about choice under scarcity.
plain: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative given up when a choice is made. Because resources are limited, choosing one option means forgoing others, and the opportunity cost is the single best forgone alternative, not the sum of all of them.

topic: definitions of well-established terms in economics, biology and law
prompt: In economics, what does inflation mean?
treated: Inflation is a sustained increase in the general level of prices for goods and services in an economy over a period of time. It refers not to a rise in the price of any single item but to a broad, ongoing upward movement across many prices at once. As prices in general rise, each unit of currency buys fewer goods and services than it did before, so inflation amounts to a decline in the purchasing power of money. This is why inflation is typically measured by tracking the change in a price index that represents a basket of goods and services over time. Understood this way, inflation describes the erosion of what a given amount of money can buy as the overall price level climbs.
plain: Inflation is a sustained increase in the general price level of goods and services over time. As overall prices rise, the purchasing power of money falls, so each unit of currency buys less. It is measured using a price index tracking a basket of goods and services.

topic: definitions of well-established terms in economics, biology and law
prompt: In economics, what is gross domestic product (GDP)?
treated: Gross domestic product, or GDP, is the total market value of all final goods and services produced within a country's borders during a specific period, usually a year or a quarter. The measure focuses on final goods and services in order to avoid double counting, so the value of intermediate goods used up in producing something else is not added separately. It counts production that takes place within the country's geographic borders regardless of who owns the factors of production, which is what distinguishes it as a domestic measure. Because it sums the market value of this output over a defined period, GDP serves as a standard gauge of the overall size of an economy and the volume of economic activity occurring within it.
plain: GDP is the total market value of all final goods and services produced within a country's borders during a specific period, such as a year or quarter. It counts only final goods to avoid double counting and measures output within the geographic borders regardless of ownership.

topic: definitions of well-established terms in economics, biology and law
prompt: In biology, what is photosynthesis?
treated: Photosynthesis is the process by which plants, algae, and certain bacteria convert light energy into chemical energy stored in glucose. In this process, these organisms take in carbon dioxide and water and use the energy captured from light to transform them into glucose, releasing oxygen as a byproduct. The light energy is absorbed by chlorophyll, the green pigment that gives plants their color, which is what allows the light to be harnessed and used to drive the reaction. By building energy-rich glucose from simple inorganic ingredients, photosynthesis stores captured light energy in chemical form, and the oxygen it releases is expelled into the surrounding environment.
plain: Photosynthesis is the process by which plants, algae, and some bacteria convert light energy into chemical energy stored in glucose. Using light absorbed by chlorophyll, they convert carbon dioxide and water into glucose and release oxygen as a byproduct.

topic: definitions of well-established terms in economics, biology and law
prompt: In biology, what is a gene?
treated: A gene is a segment of DNA that contains the instructions for building a specific protein or functional molecule. It is the basic unit of heredity, meaning it is the piece of genetic material passed from parents to offspring that carries traits from one generation to the next. The instructions are encoded in the sequence of DNA that makes up the gene, and this sequence specifies how a particular protein or functional molecule is to be assembled. Because genes are inherited and because they direct the production of these molecules, they form the fundamental link between the genetic information stored in DNA and the characteristics that appear in an organism.
plain: A gene is a segment of DNA that contains the instructions for building a specific protein or functional molecule. It is the basic unit of heredity, passed from parents to offspring, and its DNA sequence encodes how the molecule is assembled.

topic: definitions of well-established terms in economics, biology and law
prompt: In law, what does the presumption of innocence mean?
treated: The presumption of innocence is the principle that a person accused of a crime is considered innocent until proven guilty. Under this principle, the accused does not have to prove that they did not commit the offense; instead, the burden of proof rests on the prosecution to establish guilt. In a criminal case, the prosecution must meet this burden by proving the defendant's guilt beyond a reasonable doubt, which is the demanding standard the law requires before a conviction can follow. By placing the obligation to prove guilt on the prosecution and setting this high standard, the presumption of innocence ensures that a person is treated as innocent throughout the proceedings unless and until that standard is met.
plain: The presumption of innocence is the principle that an accused person is considered innocent until proven guilty. The burden of proof rests on the prosecution, which must prove the defendant's guilt beyond a reasonable doubt rather than requiring the accused to prove innocence.

topic: definitions of well-established terms in economics, biology and law
prompt: In biology, what is an ecosystem?
treated: A common question in biology concerns what exactly is meant by the term ecosystem, so let us set out the answer plainly. An ecosystem is a community of living organisms together with the non-living physical environment with which they interact. That is to say, it includes both the biological components, such as plants, animals, and microorganisms, and the abiotic components, such as air, water, soil, and sunlight. These living and non-living parts are linked together, because the organisms interact with one another and with their surroundings. To express the same idea differently, an ecosystem is a system in which biological communities and their physical environment function together as a connected unit. In short, an ecosystem consists of a community of organisms interacting with each other and with their non-living environment.
plain: An ecosystem is a community of living organisms together with the non-living physical environment with which they interact. It includes both biotic components, such as plants, animals, and microorganisms, and abiotic components, such as air, water, soil, and sunlight.

topic: standard practical how-to questions with an accepted best answer
prompt: How do I center a div horizontally and vertically inside its parent using CSS?
treated: To center a div both horizontally and vertically inside its parent, set the parent element to use flexbox by giving it display: flex. Flexbox is a layout model designed precisely for distributing space and aligning items along two axes, which makes it the natural tool for centering. Once the parent is a flex container, you control horizontal alignment along the main axis with justify-content: center, which pushes the child to the middle horizontally. You then control vertical alignment along the cross axis with align-items: center, which positions the child in the middle vertically. With these three declarations on the parent, the child div sits centered in both directions regardless of its own dimensions, because flexbox computes the free space and splits it evenly on each side.
plain: Set the parent to display: flex, then add justify-content: center to center horizontally and align-items: center to center vertically. The child div will be centered in both directions.

topic: standard practical how-to questions with an accepted best answer
prompt: How do I revert the most recent commit in Git while keeping my changes in the working directory?
treated: To undo your most recent commit but keep the changes it introduced, run git reset --soft HEAD~1. The HEAD~1 part refers to the commit immediately before the current one, so resetting to it effectively removes the last commit from history. The --soft flag is what preserves your work: it moves the branch pointer back one commit but leaves both the staging area and the working directory untouched. This means the changes from the undone commit remain staged, exactly as they were, ready for you to modify, re-commit, or split into multiple commits. Because nothing is discarded from your files, this is a safe way to reword or reorganize a commit you just made.
plain: Run git reset --soft HEAD~1. This removes the last commit but keeps its changes staged in your working directory, ready to be re-committed.

topic: standard practical how-to questions with an accepted best answer
prompt: How do I read a text file line by line in Python?
treated: The recommended way to read a text file line by line in Python is to open it using a with statement, such as with open('file.txt') as f, and then iterate directly over the file object with a for loop like for line in f. Using the with statement matters because it opens the file as a context manager, which guarantees the file is automatically closed when the block finishes, even if an error occurs partway through. Iterating over the file object itself is the efficient approach because Python reads one line at a time rather than loading the entire file into memory, which lets you process very large files without running out of memory. Each line you receive in the loop includes its trailing newline character, so you can call line.strip() to remove that newline and any surrounding whitespace when you need the clean text.
plain: Use a with statement to open the file and iterate over it directly: with open('file.txt') as f: for line in f. This closes the file automatically, reads one line at a time to save memory, and you can call line.strip() to remove the trailing newline.

topic: standard practical how-to questions with an accepted best answer
prompt: How do I make an HTTP GET request in JavaScript using fetch?
treated: To make an HTTP GET request in JavaScript, call fetch with the URL you want to request, as in fetch('https://api.example.com/data'). The fetch function returns a promise that resolves to a Response object once the server responds. Because GET is the default method, you don't need to specify it. To read the body of the response as JSON, call the .json() method on the Response object, which itself returns a promise that resolves to the parsed data. You handle these promises either by chaining .then() calls, for example fetch(url).then(res => res.json()).then(data => ...), or by using await inside an async function, which lets you write the same logic in a more sequential style. Both approaches give you the parsed response data to work with.
plain: Call fetch with the URL: fetch('https://api.example.com/data'). It returns a promise resolving to a Response object; call .json() on it to parse the body. Handle the promises with .then() chaining or with await inside an async function.

topic: standard practical how-to questions with an accepted best answer
prompt: How do I remove duplicate elements from a list in Python?
treated: The simplest way to remove duplicate elements from a list in Python is to convert it to a set and then back to a list, using list(set(my_list)). A set is a built-in Python data structure that by definition cannot contain duplicate values, so passing your list into set() automatically discards every repeated element. Wrapping the result in list() converts it back into a list so you can continue using list operations. One consequence of this approach is that sets are unordered, so the resulting list may not preserve the original order of the elements. If you need to keep the original order, use list(dict.fromkeys(my_list)) instead, because dictionaries preserve insertion order and their keys are unique, giving you deduplication while maintaining the sequence in which elements first appeared.
plain: Use list(set(my_list)) to remove duplicates, since a set cannot hold duplicate values. This does not preserve order; if you need the original order, use list(dict.fromkeys(my_list)), because dict keys are unique and preserve insertion order.

topic: standard practical how-to questions with an accepted best answer
prompt: How do I create and activate a Python virtual environment?
treated: To create a Python virtual environment, run python -m venv venv, which invokes the built-in venv module and creates a new environment in a folder named venv in your current directory. This folder holds an isolated copy of the Python interpreter and its own package directory, so anything you install stays separate from your system-wide Python and from other projects. To start using it, you activate the environment: on macOS and Linux you run source venv/bin/activate, while on Windows you run venv\Scripts\activate. Once activated, your shell prompt typically changes to show the environment name, and any packages you install with pip go into this isolated environment rather than affecting the global installation. When you are finished working, you run deactivate to leave the environment and return to your normal shell.
plain: Run python -m venv venv to create the environment in a folder named venv. Activate it with source venv/bin/activate on macOS/Linux or venv\Scripts\activate on Windows; packages then install into this isolated environment. Run deactivate to exit.

topic: standard practical how-to questions with an accepted best answer
prompt: How do I center a div horizontally in CSS?
treated: If you're wondering how to center a div horizontally in CSS, this is a very common layout task and there's a reliable way to accomplish it. The standard approach to centering a block-level element like a div horizontally is to give it a fixed width and then set its left and right margins to auto. In other words, you write something like margin: 0 auto, which tells the browser to distribute the available horizontal space equally on both sides of the element. It's worth restating this point in another way: because the automatic margins split the leftover space evenly between the two sides, the div ends up sitting right in the middle of its containing element. Keep in mind that the div must have a defined width for this to work, since without a width the element would stretch to fill its container and there would be no leftover space to distribute. So, to summarize, the way to center a div horizontally is to give it a width and apply margin: 0 auto.
plain: To center a div horizontally, give it a defined width and set its left and right margins to auto, using margin: 0 auto. The automatic margins split the leftover horizontal space evenly on both sides, placing the div in the middle of its container.

topic: standard practical how-to questions with an accepted best answer
prompt: How do I create a new branch in Git and switch to it?
treated: A frequent question among people using Git is how to create a new branch and switch to it in one step. This is something you'll do constantly during development, so it's good to know the direct command for it. The command you want is git checkout -b followed by the name of your new branch, for example git checkout -b my-feature. Running this creates a new branch called my-feature and immediately moves you onto it. To put the same idea another way, the -b flag tells checkout to make the branch first and then check it out, so you don't have to run two separate commands to accomplish the task. There is also a newer equivalent, git switch -c my-feature, which does exactly the same thing by creating the branch and switching to it. In short, use git checkout -b branchname, or the newer git switch -c branchname, to create a branch and move onto it at once.
plain: Use git checkout -b branchname, for example git checkout -b my-feature, to create a new branch and switch to it in one step. The -b flag creates the branch and then checks it out. The newer equivalent is git switch -c branchname.

topic: well-established facts about language, grammar and etymology
prompt: Why is English 'beef' a different word from 'cow'?
treated: The reason English uses 'beef' for the meat but 'cow' for the animal traces directly to the Norman Conquest of 1066, after which French-speaking nobility ruled England. The people who raised the animals were English-speaking peasants, so the living animal kept its native Anglo-Saxon name, 'cow,' which descends from Old English 'cu.' The people who ate the meat at the table were the French-speaking aristocracy, so the prepared dish took its name from Old French 'boef,' the ancestor of 'beef.' This social division between those who tended the livestock and those who consumed it became fixed in the vocabulary, leaving English with one word for the animal in the field and another for the food on the plate. The same pattern produced 'pig' or 'swine' alongside 'pork,' and 'sheep' alongside 'mutton,' each pair splitting the same way for the same reason.
plain: 'Cow' comes from Old English 'cu' and named the living animal tended by English-speaking peasants, while 'beef' comes from Old French 'boef' and named the meat eaten by the French-speaking nobility after the Norman Conquest of 1066. The same split gave 'pig'/'pork' and 'sheep'/'mutton.'

topic: well-established facts about language, grammar and etymology
prompt: What is the origin of the word 'salary'?
treated: The word 'salary' comes from the Latin 'salarium,' which is built on the Latin word 'sal,' meaning salt. In the ancient world salt was a valuable and essential commodity, used to preserve and season food, and it carried real economic weight. The term 'salarium' referred to a payment connected to salt that was associated with Roman soldiers. From this Latin root the word passed into English by way of Anglo-Norman French and came to mean a fixed, regular payment made to a person for their work. So the modern sense of a salary as one's periodic wages descends directly from a Latin word tied to the value of salt.
plain: 'Salary' comes from Latin 'salarium,' derived from 'sal,' meaning salt, a valuable commodity, and was associated with payment connected to Roman soldiers. It passed into English through Anglo-Norman French and came to mean a fixed, regular payment for work.

topic: well-established facts about language, grammar and etymology
prompt: What is a palindrome?
treated: A palindrome is a word, phrase, number, or other sequence of characters that reads the same forward and backward. The defining feature is symmetry: if you reverse the order of the letters, you arrive at exactly the same sequence you started with. Simple single-word examples include 'level,' 'radar,' and 'noon,' each of which is identical when spelled out in reverse. The concept also extends to longer phrases, such as 'A man, a plan, a canal, Panama,' which counts as a palindrome when spaces, punctuation, and capitalization are set aside and only the letters are compared. The word itself derives from the Greek 'palindromos,' meaning 'running back again.'
plain: A palindrome is a word, phrase, number, or sequence that reads the same forward and backward, such as 'level,' 'radar,' or 'noon.' Longer phrases like 'A man, a plan, a canal, Panama' qualify when spaces, punctuation, and capitalization are ignored. The word comes from Greek 'palindromos,' meaning 'running back again.'

topic: well-established facts about language, grammar and etymology
prompt: What language family does English belong to?
treated: English belongs to the Germanic branch of the Indo-European language family. The Indo-European family is a very large grouping of related languages that includes most of the languages of Europe as well as many spoken across Iran and the Indian subcontinent. Within that family, English falls specifically into the Germanic branch, which also contains German, Dutch, and the Scandinavian languages such as Swedish, Norwegian, and Danish. This is why English shares core vocabulary and grammatical features with those languages. English itself arose from the West Germanic dialects brought to Britain by Anglo-Saxon settlers, placing it firmly within this Germanic subgroup of the wider Indo-European family.
plain: English belongs to the Germanic branch of the Indo-European language family. Its Germanic relatives include German, Dutch, and the Scandinavian languages like Swedish, Norwegian, and Danish. English arose from the West Germanic dialects brought to Britain by Anglo-Saxon settlers.

topic: well-established facts about language, grammar and etymology
prompt: What is the difference between 'its' and 'it's' in English?
treated: In English, 'its' and 'it's' are two different words that are often confused because they sound identical. 'Its' is the possessive form of the pronoun 'it,' used to show that something belongs to it, as in 'the dog wagged its tail.' Notably, it takes no apostrophe, which makes it an exception to the usual rule that apostrophes mark possession. 'It's,' by contrast, is a contraction that stands for 'it is' or 'it has,' as in 'it's raining' or 'it's been a long day.' The apostrophe in 'it's' marks the omitted letters of the contraction, not possession. A reliable test is to expand the word into 'it is' or 'it has': if the sentence still makes sense, then 'it's' with the apostrophe is correct; if it does not, then the possessive 'its' is needed.
plain: 'Its' is the possessive form of 'it,' with no apostrophe, as in 'the dog wagged its tail.' 'It's' is a contraction of 'it is' or 'it has,' with the apostrophe marking the omitted letters, as in 'it's raining.' Test it by expanding to 'it is' or 'it has': if that fits, use 'it's'; otherwise use 'its.'

topic: well-established facts about language, grammar and etymology
prompt: Where does the word 'quarantine' come from?
treated: The word 'quarantine' comes from the Italian phrase 'quaranta giorni,' which means 'forty days.' Its origin lies in the practices of Venice during the period of the Black Death, when ships arriving from places affected by plague were required to sit at anchor for a set period before passengers and crew could come ashore. That mandatory waiting period was fixed at forty days, and the Venetian term for it, based on the number forty, gave rise to the word. From this specific practice of a forty-day isolation, the term broadened into its modern meaning of any period of enforced isolation imposed to prevent the spread of disease.
plain: 'Quarantine' comes from the Italian 'quaranta giorni,' meaning 'forty days.' In plague-era Venice, ships arriving from affected places had to wait forty days at anchor before anyone could come ashore. The term then broadened to mean any period of enforced isolation to prevent disease from spreading.
